boundary_note: Bounded first pass for the frozen Secessionville record (June 16, 1862) in Operations Against Charleston [June 1862]. The June 2-15 landing and skirmishing on James Island, the May 29 Pocotaligo expedition and the later evacuation of the island are context. Campaign-wide marches, reinforcements, returns and multi-action loss totals are context; they are not assigned to one record or added across records. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.rationale: No inspected return establishes matched personnel at a common opening boundary. Imported numerical estimates remain unchanged; this pass does not validate them as simultaneous opening forces.

claims.value: The frozen force text and the live page both read 8,600 total (US 6,600; CS 2,000). Benham's June 16 report says about 3,500 of Stevens's command with four guns led the advance and about 3,100 of Wright's and Williams's commands with six guns supported on the left. Jones gives the June 9 consolidated morning reports for the whole Federal force on James Island as 9472 (Wright 3232, Stevens 4313, Williams 1927), says the defenders of the works were believed to be fewer than 500, and gives the Secessionville garrison as two artillery companies and two infantry battalions, in all less than five hundred, joined early in the assault by a detachment of one hundred men and later by McEnery's battalion; Evans had ordered the post reinforced up to 2000 men, but those reinforcements had not arrived.
claims.rationale: Benham's two approximations sum to the frozen US 6,600, but no inspected passage states how the frozen figures were derived. Jones's 9472 is a different population and date (all Federal troops on the island, June 9); his Confederate figures are garrison scopes before reinforcement. None is adopted as a matched opening strength.

claims.value: Jones says the works in front of Secessionville occupied the most contracted part of a narrow neck of land between brush-fringed marshes, with a front of attack about one hundred yards long, approached over cultivated fields bordered with hedges; he says the attempt to charge with brigade front over ground scarcely wide enough for a regiment crowded the regiments into the marshes. Benham says the Secessionville batteries covered the whole of the Union position and camps.
claims.rationale: Ground described by a history and an interested report; no map verification. The works predate the attack; the assault formation was the attackers' choice.

claims.value: Benham says the fort appeared to grow stronger daily. Jones says Benham had been told that trains loaded with troops had been seen entering Charleston, that the attackers surprised the picket in its house, and that Lamar had observed enough to expect an attack in the night of the 15th or early the next morning and so reported to Evans, but let his exhausted men sleep at three o'clock. Benham reports the pickets captured as a lieutenant and 4 men; Jones says two or three.
claims.rationale: Attributed knowledge from an interested report and a history; no message log inspected. No original reconnaissance, order or message chain was inspected to establish contemporary knowledge. Surprise in a summary does not independently establish what each commander knew.

claims.value: Benham writes that Hunter had approved his view that the fort and floating battery at Secessionville had to be destroyed or captured to secure the camps, and that he ordered a reconnaissance in force to capture and hold the fort if it proved not too strong. Jones quotes Hunter's written instructions of the 10th forbidding any advance on Charleston or attack on Fort Johnson until reinforced while providing for a secure entrenched encampment, and says Benham decided to assault at dawn. NPS says the attack was contrary to Hunter's orders.
claims.rationale: Contested statements of intent and authority; the question whether the attack exceeded Hunter's instructions is not resolved here.

claims.value: Benham accompanied Wright's supporting column and ordered the withdrawal about 9 a.m., crediting Stevens's dispositions. Jones says Stevens objected to a night assault and was overruled by Benham, that Wright was ordered not to renew a repulsed assault, and that Hunter relieved Benham and sent him to Washington in arrest for disobedience of orders. On the Confederate side Jones says Lamar commanded the post and aimed the columbiad himself, Evans commanded on the island, and Hagood sent reinforcements and asked Evans for leave to attack Williams's flank. The frozen commanders are Brigadier Generals Henry Benham (US) and Nathan Evans (CS).
claims.rationale: Command roles from an interested report and a history; neither listed commander receives automatic sole credit.

claims.value: The frozen and live results read Confederate victory. Benham says the infantry could make no marked impression on the fort and that he withdrew the troops, the main object of the reconnaissance having been accomplished; Jones calls the assault a disastrous failure after a conflict Stevens timed at twenty-five minutes, followed by the Union evacuation of James Island.
claims.rationale: Retain the original result and engagement interval; later movements and campaign contribution are different measures. No new probabilities or individual causal credit. Benham's description of the attack as a reconnaissance is his own framing.

claims.value: The frozen casualty text reads 889 total (US 685; CS 204); the live field reads 887 (US 683; CS 204). Jones gives an aggregate Federal loss of 683 and a Confederate loss of 204. Benham's same-day report estimated Stevens's loss at about 450 (7 officers and 46 men killed, 14 officers and 307 men wounded, 2 officers and about 150 missing) and Wright's and Williams's at about 150, expecting the total to be much within 600.
claims.rationale: Original casualty returns were not inspected; preserve totals, categories, cutoffs and differences. No canonical reconciliation or casualty-based opening count; related actions must not be added without resolving population overlap. Benham's figures are incomplete same-day estimates, not a return.

open_questions: Hunter's June 23 report (read, not selected), the Union casualty return (No. 2), Wright's, Stevens's and subordinate reports, Evans's, Lamar's, Hagood's and other Confederate reports and the Confederate casualty return remain deferred.

NPS/CWSAC (NPS battle page and frozen Arnold rows) is one family. Henry W. Benham's June 16, 1862 report (Official Records I, XIV, No. 3) is an interested Union account written before his relief. Samuel Jones's The Siege of Charleston (1911) is a posthumous Confederate general's history that quotes Union and Confederate reports and is not independent of them. Official Records volumes are shared containers, not additional witnesses. Report dates are not event times or proof of contemporary knowledge.
No automatic commander attribution, causal campaign score, morale/readiness number or battle/campaign double counting.
